title: Foundation Repair Cost in the Bay Area: What You'll Actually Pay in 2026 (By Method and Damage Level)
metaTitle: Foundation Repair Cost Bay Area (2026) | Real Prices by Method
excerpt: Foundation repair in the Bay Area typically runs $5,000 for minor crack injection to $80,000+ for full underpinning. Here's what each method costs, which one your home actually needs, and the questions to ask before signing anything.
secondaryKeywords: how much does foundation repair cost

outline.h2: The Short Answer: Bay Area Foundation Repair Cost Ranges
outline.notes: Crack injection $500-$2,500. Seismic bolting / soft-story retrofit $5,000-$15,000 (Brace + Bolt eligible for $3K grant). Partial underpinning (4-8 piers) $12,000-$30,000. Full underpinning (10-20 piers) $30,000-$80,000+. House leveling / re-shimming $8,000-$25,000. Method matters more than total — most homes don't need the most expensive option.

outline.h2: What Foundation Problem Do You Actually Have?
outline.notes: Diagnostic framework. Diagonal cracks from window/door corners = settling. Horizontal cracks in stem walls = lateral pressure. Stair-step cracks in brick/stucco = differential settlement. Sloping floors measured with a marble test. Sticking doors on one side of house. Explain that a house that survived 1989 Loma Prieta may still be soft-story vulnerable — separate issue from active settlement.

outline.h2: Repair Method 1: Crack Injection ($500–$2,500)
outline.notes: Epoxy or polyurethane injection into non-structural cracks. Appropriate for: hairline cracks in stem walls, cosmetic cracks in slabs, moisture intrusion at cold joints. Not appropriate for: active movement, structural cracks over 1/4 inch. Cost per crack: $300-$800. Lifespan of repair: permanent if underlying movement has stopped.

outline.h2: Repair Method 2: Seismic Retrofit / Brace + Bolt ($5,000–$15,000)
h3: What Bolting and Bracing Actually Does
SF Earthquake Brace + Bolt $3,000 Grant Program
Which Homes Qualify (Pre-1980 Cripple Wall Homes)
outline.notes: Not repair — prevention. Bolts sill plate to foundation, adds plywood shear panels to cripple walls. Typical SF Victorian/Edwardian: $6,000-$12,000. Brace + Bolt grant covers $3,000 for eligible pre-1980 homes with cripple walls in participating cities (SF, Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, others). Cost after grant often $3,000-$9,000. Reference the ABAG-run program by name.

outline.h2: Repair Method 3: Underpinning ($12,000–$80,000+)
outline.notes: Brief overview only — link to the deeper underpinning post. Helical piers, push piers, slabjacking. When it's needed vs when contractors oversell it. Marina fill and Sunset clay examples. Cross-link to /blog/foundation-underpinning-cost-san-francisco.

outline.h2: Repair Method 4: House Leveling and Re-Shimming ($8,000–$25,000)
outline.notes: For homes on post-and-pier or perimeter foundations where the house has settled but the foundation itself is sound. Jack the house, add new shims/posts, adjust for level. Common on Bernal Heights Victorians and Berkeley bungalows. Faster and cheaper than underpinning when the foundation itself isn't failing.

outline.h2: What Drives Cost Up in the Bay Area
h3: SF DBI / Oakland Planning & Building / Berkeley Planning Permits
Soil Testing on Fill and Bay Mud
outline.notes: Engineering $3K-$8K. Permits vary by jurisdiction — SF DBI $2K-$5K, Oakland $1.5K-$4K, Berkeley $1.5K-$4K. Soil testing (required on Marina fill, Mission Bay, parts of West Berkeley) $2K-$5K.

outline.h2: Red Flags in Foundation Repair Bids
outline.notes: 1. Free inspection that ends in same-day 'sign now for a discount.' 2. Quotes without an engineer's stamp for underpinning. 3. Slabjacking recommended for whole-house settlement (wrong tool). 4. Bids that don't line-item engineering, permits, or contingency. 5. Warranty language that's verbal only. 6. No specific pier count and depth. 7. Contractor won't name the specific method.

title: Seismic Retrofit Cost in San Francisco & the Bay Area: Brace + Bolt, Soft-Story, and What You Actually Need
metaTitle: Seismic Retrofit Cost SF Bay Area (2026) | Brace + Bolt Guide
excerpt: Seismic retrofit in the Bay Area runs $5,000 to $15,000 for most single-family homes — and a $3,000 Brace + Bolt grant covers a big chunk. Here's what your home needs, what qualifies for the grant, and how to spot a contractor overselling you.

outline.h2: The Short Answer: Bay Area Seismic Retrofit Costs
outline.notes: Standard cripple wall + bolting retrofit for a typical SF single-family: $6,000-$12,000. Soft-story multi-unit retrofit: $60,000-$250,000+. Brace + Bolt grant covers $3,000 for eligible pre-1980 homes. After grant, most single-family retrofits net $3,000-$9,000.

outline.h2: What Seismic Retrofit Actually Is (And Isn't)
outline.notes: Retrofit doesn't repair damage — it prevents it. Two main components: (1) anchor bolts connect the wooden sill plate to the concrete foundation, (2) plywood shear panels stiffen the cripple wall (the short wall between foundation and first floor). Together they prevent the house from sliding off its foundation in an earthquake — the exact failure mode that destroyed thousands of Bay Area homes in 1906, 1989, and 2014 Napa quakes.

outline.h2: Does Your Home Actually Need It?
h3: Pre-1980 Homes with Cripple Walls (Almost Always Yes)
outline.notes: Most Bay Area homes built before 1980 have cripple walls and were built before seismic code required bolting. Victorian and Edwardian rowhouses in SF (Noe Valley, Alamo Square, Mission, Richmond) are highest priority. Doelger homes in the Sunset and Daly City Westlake — mixed, some have partial bolting. Craftsman bungalows in Berkeley Elmwood and Oakland Rockridge — high priority. Concrete slab ranches — usually don't have cripple walls, retrofit not applicable.

outline.h2: The Earthquake Brace + Bolt Program ($3,000 Grant)
h3: Timeline From Application to Grant Payment
outline.notes: Program administered by ABAG (Association of Bay Area Governments) and CEA (California Earthquake Authority). Participating: SF, Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, Piedmont, El Cerrito, Albany, San Leandro, others. Qualification: pre-1980, single-family or duplex, cripple wall construction, raised foundation, on level ground. Application windows open annually — check earthquakebracebolt.com. Grant paid after inspection confirms completion.

outline.h2: Soft-Story Retrofit: The Multi-Unit Version
outline.notes: Soft-story = ground floor with parking or storefront and wood-frame residential above. First floor lacks shear walls, collapses in earthquakes. SF DBI Administrative Bulletin AB-094 mandates retrofit for buildings with 5+ residential units built pre-1978 with soft-story condition — most compliance deadlines passed but new acquisitions still trigger the requirement. Cost by units: 5-9 units $60K-$120K, 10-15 units $120K-$200K, 20+ units $200K-$400K+.

outline.h2: Real Cost Examples From Recent Projects
outline.notes: Three examples with specifics: (1) 1918 Noe Valley Victorian, full perimeter bolting + cripple wall retrofit, $9,800 gross / $6,800 after grant, 5 days work. (2) Berkeley Elmwood 1925 Craftsman, partial bolting only (existing plywood on cripple), $6,400 gross / $3,400 net, 3 days. (3) Bernal Heights 1908 Edwardian on slope, engineered solution with hillside bracing, $16,500 (didn't qualify for grant due to slope), 8 days. Each with what drove the cost.

title: Do You Need a Permit for Your Deck? SF, Marin, Berkeley, and Oakland Rules Explained
metaTitle: Deck Permit Requirements SF, Marin, Berkeley, Oakland (2026)
excerpt: Bay Area deck permits are triggered by height, size, and location — and every jurisdiction has different rules. Here's what actually requires a permit in SF, Marin, Berkeley, and Oakland, what it costs, and what happens if you skip it.
secondaryKeywords: do i need a permit for a deck

outline.h2: The Short Answer: When You Need a Deck Permit in the Bay Area
outline.notes: Universal rule across most Bay Area jurisdictions: decks over 30 inches above grade require a permit. Below that, most (but not all) jurisdictions exempt them. Attached decks almost always require a permit regardless of height because they connect to the house structure. Marin, SF, Berkeley, and Oakland each have subtle rule differences that matter for real projects.

outline.h2: The Universal Trigger: 30 Inches Above Grade
outline.notes: The California Residential Code (CRC) sets the baseline: any deck, platform, or walking surface more than 30 inches above the adjacent grade at any point requires a building permit. This isn't jurisdiction-specific — it's state code. But many cities have additional local triggers below 30 inches: square footage limits, attachment to house, structural modifications.

outline.h2: San Francisco Deck Permit Rules (SF DBI)
outline.notes: SF Department of Building Inspection (DBI) requires permits for: any deck 30+ inches above grade, any deck attached to the house, any deck over 200 sq ft, any deck with a roof or pergola. Permit cost: $400-$2,500 for typical residential deck. Timeline: 4-12 weeks depending on plan complexity. Historic districts (Alamo Square, Haight-Ashbury, Presidio Heights) trigger additional Planning review adding 4-8 weeks. Steep sites often require structural engineer stamp ($2K-$5K extra).

outline.h2: Marin County & City Deck Permit Rules
h3: Mill Valley, Sausalito, Tiburon Municipal Rules
outline.notes: Marin CDA governs unincorporated county areas. Incorporated cities (Mill Valley, Sausalito, Tiburon, San Rafael, Larkspur, Ross) each have their own building departments. Common Marin quirks: view ordinances in Tiburon and parts of Mill Valley add design review, WUI fire zone requires non-combustible or ignition-resistant deck materials (composite generally OK, some restrictions on lattice and stairs). Permit costs: $600-$3,500. Timeline: 6-16 weeks — Marin runs longer than SF.

outline.h2: Oakland & Berkeley Deck Permit Rules
outline.notes: Oakland: standard 30-inch trigger, plus any deck in a landslide hazard zone requires geotechnical review. Hillside areas (Oakland Hills, Montclair, Piedmont Ave adjacent) trigger extra review. Permit cost $500-$2,000 typical. Berkeley: similar rules, Berkeley Hills WUI fire zone requires non-combustible materials, permit cost $500-$1,800. Both cities have 4-10 week timelines for standard residential decks.

outline.h2: What Happens If You Skip the Permit
outline.notes: Bad outcomes: (1) home insurance denies claims on unpermitted structures if they cause damage. (2) sale of home flags unpermitted deck at inspection, buyer demands price reduction ($10K-$40K typical) or requires legalization. (3) legalization retroactively costs 2-3x normal permit fees plus tear-open inspection for hidden framing. (4) neighbor complaint triggers stop-work order and daily fines. (5) failed structural — unpermitted decks disproportionately fail because they skip structural review. Real number: SF DBI cites 200+ unpermitted deck cases per year.
